content: The recommendations provide detailed guidance on delivering high-quality family planning services. These services encompass a range of critical areas, including contraceptive services, pregnancy testing and counseling, assistance for clients seeking to achieve pregnancy, basic infertility services, preconception health services, and sexually transmitted disease (STD) services. The primary audience for this report includes all current or potential providers of family planning services. This includes those working in dedicated family planning service sites, as well as private and public providers offering more comprehensive primary care services. The United States continues to face significant challenges in improving reproductive health outcomes. Nearly half of all pregnancies are unintended, with over 700,000 adolescents aged 15–19 becoming pregnant annually, and more than 300,000 giving birth. Additionally, one in eight pregnancies in the U.S. results in preterm birth, and infant mortality rates remain high compared to other developed nations. These outcomes disproportionately affect racial and ethnic minority populations. This report aims to assist primary care providers in offering family planning services that help individuals and couples achieve their desired number and spacing of children while increasing the likelihood of healthy births. It emphasizes the importance of offering a full range of contraceptive methods, addressing the unique needs of adolescent clients, and using family planning visits to provide selected preventive health services for women, in alignment with recommendations from the Institute of Medicine and adopted by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The recommendations were collaboratively developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Office of Population Affairs (OPA) within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Family planning services include providing contraception to help individuals plan and space births, prevent unintended pregnancies, and reduce the number of abortions. They also involve offering pregnancy testing and counseling, assisting clients who wish to conceive, providing basic infertility services, delivering preconception health services to improve maternal and infant outcomes, and offering STD screening and treatment to prevent tubal infertility and improve overall health. The recommendations integrate evidence-based guidance from the CDC on the safe provision of contraceptive methods for women with various medical conditions. They also incorporate recommendations from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) on STD prevention, preconception care, and related preventive health services. It also emphasizes the need for culturally competent care to meet the diverse needs of all clients, including adolescents, individuals with limited English proficiency, those with disabilities, and LGBTQ individuals. The recommendations stress the importance of timely service delivery, efficient use of resources, and equitable access to high-quality care for all clients, regardless of personal characteristics such as race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status. The development of these recommendations involved a rigorous, multistage process, including systematic reviews of the literature, input from technical panels of subject matter experts, and feedback from an Expert Work Group familiar with family planning service delivery. The recommendations were finalized based on the quality of evidence, potential health outcomes, cost considerations, and implementation feasibility. The report is intended to guide general clinical practice while allowing for adaptation to meet the specific needs of diverse populations, such as clients who are HIV-positive or substance users. It provides a framework for assessing client needs and determining appropriate family planning services, including contraceptive services, pregnancy testing and counseling, and assistance with achieving pregnancy. Providers are encouraged to integrate family planning services into broader preventive health care frameworks, ensuring that clients receive comprehensive care tailored to their individual circumstances. This includes addressing the needs of clients seeking to prevent or achieve pregnancy, as well as those visiting for other health concerns, such as acute or chronic care. The recommendations also emphasize the importance of preconception health services, which promote the health of individuals of reproductive age before conception to improve pregnancy-related outcomes. These services are beneficial even for those who do not intend to become pregnant, as they enhance overall health and well-being. Finally, the report provides detailed guidance on delivering contraceptive services, including offering a full range of FDA-approved methods, conducting brief assessments to identify safe options for clients, providing contraceptive counseling to support informed decision-making, and ensuring access to selected methods, preferably on-site or through referral if necessary.
